title: Deformation arguments
purpose: Replace a difficult object by an easier one while preserving the answer.
first_principles: This family begins by deciding what moves are legal. Then it moves the picture until the answer is easier to see. The proof lives in the guarantee that the motion did not change the feature being asked about.

depth.human_problem: The human problem is that the original picture is often too tangled to reason about directly, but an uncontrolled simplification can answer the wrong question. The family asks how to change the picture while keeping the exact data the problem cares about.
depth.first_principles: Start by naming the legal moves and the fixed data. Then move the object through those moves until it is easier to inspect. If endpoints, boundaries, gluing rules, forbidden crossings, side behavior, or a protected count survive every step, the simplified picture speaks for the original picture and not merely for itself.
depth.how_it_works: A deformation proof has four parts: the starting object, the contract of allowed motion, the protected feature, and the simpler endpoint. The proof fails if any part is left unnamed or unchecked. The endpoint is convincing only because the route to it was legal and carried the protected feature all the way.
depth.course_examples: The disk-connection puzzle, surface classification by surgery, intersection invariance, and the treatment of vector-field defects all use this family. In each case, motion is not a side effect; it is the proof method.
depth.failure_mode: The common failure is to simplify by a move that the problem does not permit. Cutting a loop, sliding an endpoint, passing through an obstacle, or changing a boundary condition may make the picture easier while solving the wrong problem.

essay: Deformation arguments are the course's way of replacing a hard object by an easier one without losing the question. The first step is not to move anything. The first step is to state the contract: what may bend, what must stay attached, which crossings are forbidden, which endpoints stay fixed, and which boundaries still count as boundaries. Only after that contract is clear does motion become a proof method.

The family matters because many topological questions are impossible to settle from the first drawing. A tangled drawing may hide a simple answer; a simple-looking drawing may hide an obstruction. Deformation gives the reader permission to simplify, but only under rules that preserve the feature being tested. This is why the endpoint of a deformation proof is not evidence by itself. The evidence is the whole legal journey from the original picture to the easier one.

From first principles, deformation separates appearance from obligation. Appearance is the visible wiggle, bend, angle, or placement. Obligation is the part the problem refuses to let go: boundary order, no crossing, one-sidedness, a signed total, or the meaning of a map. A deformation proof moves the appearance while guarding the obligation. If the obligation survives, the easier picture can answer the harder one.

This family connects the early disk-path puzzle to later vector-field cleanup. In the disk puzzle, the protected data include endpoint order and the no-crossing rule. In surface surgery, the protected data include the surface being studied and the effect of each cut or gluing step. In vector-field cleanup, the protected data include the total index unless a controlled event explains how local defects change. The proof is not saying that all drawings are equally good. It is saying that the allowed drawings form a connected range of possibilities, and the protected fact stays the same throughout that range. The reader should therefore ask for the route, not only the before-and-after pictures.

The mathematical principle is plain: if every allowed step preserves the relevant fact, then the final easy picture can speak for the original hard picture. The danger is equally plain: one illegal step can make the final picture irrelevant. Deformation works because its freedom is disciplined.

contract.input: A hard picture whose exact drawing is less important than the rule it carries: a route, boundary order, side behavior, gluing instruction, forbidden crossing, or count. The input must name the thing being moved and the data that are not allowed to move. A path with fixed endpoints, for example, is not the same input as a loose curve.
contract.action: State the legal moves before moving anything. Then move the object through only those moves, checking the in-between states as well as the final picture. Each move has to preserve the named question: the proof may bend, slide, or redraw the picture, but it may not win by cutting, crossing forbidden matter, or changing the setup.
contract.evidence: The protected evidence is the fact that survives the whole motion: same endpoints, same boundary data, same route relation, same gluing, same side behavior, or same invariant. The evidence is not the cleaned-up endpoint. The evidence is the survival of the named fact during the entire legal journey.
contract.output: The output is a simpler picture that can answer the original question because the legal path to it preserved that question. The result is the original problem seen in a readable form, with a record of why the simplification did not rewrite the problem.
contract.failure_test: Reject the argument if it cuts, glues, passes through forbidden matter, moves fixed data, skips an in-between state, or changes the meaning of sameness. One illegal step disconnects the final picture from the starting problem, even if the final picture looks convincing.

playbook.setup: Start with the original object, not the cleaned-up target picture. Mark the fixed data before any simplification: endpoints, boundary pieces, obstacles, gluing rules, side choices, forbidden crossings, and the question being protected. Also name the carrier of the motion, because a path, loop, surface, field, and state space each have different legal moves.
playbook.move: Move the object continuously through only the allowed changes. Check the in-between states, not only the start and finish. After each kind of move, say why the protected fact has not changed, why no forbidden event was crossed, and why the motion still belongs to the same problem.
playbook.payoff: The final simpler picture answers the original problem because the legal route to it carried the same question all the way across. The simplified picture is evidence only through that route; without the route, it is just another drawing with no right to speak for the starting object.
playbook.failure: The method fails when the easy picture is reached by crossing through a forbidden object, moving fixed data, skipping intermediate states, or silently changing what sameness means. Then the final picture may be readable, but it answers a different question and cannot be used as evidence for the original one.
playbook.reader_test: Can the reader describe the full legal route, name one tempting illegal shortcut, identify the in-between event where that shortcut breaks the rules, and state what fact was preserved along the route at every step?

title: Surviving-count arguments
purpose: Find a number or sign that legal moves cannot alter.
first_principles: This family turns shape into accounting. It counts pieces, holes, crossings, turns, or defects in a way that cancels fake changes and keeps the real obstruction.

depth.human_problem: The human problem is that a drawing can change while the underlying obstruction remains. A count gives the reader something stable enough to compare before and after the change, but only if it was designed for the changes the problem permits.
depth.first_principles: Do not count everything that is visible. First list the legal local changes: subdividing a cell, creating two crossings, sliding a defect, reversing a side choice, or passing through a controlled special moment. Then count the feature whose changes cancel under those moves. Sometimes the count is alternating, as in Euler characteristic. Sometimes it is signed, as in intersection number or index. Sometimes parity is enough because only even changes can occur.
depth.how_it_works: A surviving-count proof identifies which local changes can happen, then shows those changes leave the chosen total alone. After that local audit, one honest computation in an easy picture constrains every legally related picture and can forbid a desired outcome or force at least one event.
depth.course_examples: Euler characteristic counts cells with alternating signs. Intersection number counts meetings with plus and minus signs. Poincare-Hopf counts vector-field defects and ties their total to the surface. These are different objects but the same proof instinct.
depth.failure_mode: The common failure is to use a count that changes under harmless redrawings. A raw crossing count, for example, can rise or fall when a canceling pair is created, so it is not the protected quantity.

essay: Surviving-count arguments begin with a practical problem: the visible picture changes too much. Crossings can appear, cells can be subdivided, arrows can be redrawn, and defects can move. A raw count of everything usually fails because it records accidental clutter. The course therefore asks for a count designed to ignore the harmless changes while keeping the obstruction that matters.

Euler characteristic does this by alternating pieces. Intersection number does this by using signs. Vector-field index does this by recording how arrows turn around a defect. Parity does it more coarsely by keeping only evenness or oddness. These examples look different on the surface, but they share one idea: count the part of the situation that legal motion cannot erase.

From first principles, the count is engineered around the allowed local changes. If a face is split, the added edge and face must cancel in the Euler account. If two intersections are born together, their signs must add to zero. If a vector-field defect splits into pieces, the local indices must keep the same total. The count is not chosen because it looks important; it is chosen because the harmless changes leave it alone.

A good count can prove impossibility or forced existence without listing every possible drawing. Once the count is known in one honest version of the object, every legally related version has to obey it. If the total is odd, at least one event must remain. If the signed total is nonzero, complete cancellation is impossible. If the Euler account is fixed, any decomposition of the same surface must pay the same final bill. That is why a small number can carry a large conclusion: it represents all legal redrawings, not one snapshot.

The reader should test every surviving-count argument by asking what one allowed change does to the total. If the proof cannot explain that local event, the count has not earned trust. If it can, the arithmetic becomes a way to hold the whole moving picture still.

contract.input: A situation where visible local events change too easily: cells split, crossings appear, defects move, arrows turn, or raw counts fluctuate. The input must include both the local event being counted and the list of legal ways that event can change. Without that list, the count has no survival test.
contract.action: Design a count that ignores harmless changes by cancellation, alternating terms, parity, or signs with geometric meaning. The design must match the legal local changes. If a pair of crossings can appear together, the count must know whether they cancel; if a cell is subdivided, the count must know which new pieces offset each other.
contract.evidence: The protected evidence is the total that legal redrawings cannot change, even though individual local events may appear or disappear. The total remembers forced structure rather than clutter because the harmless changes have already been audited one local move at a time.
contract.output: The output is a number, sign total, or parity fact that can prove impossibility, force existence, or compare two legally related pictures. One honest computation then applies across all legal versions because the count has already shown it survives the permitted changes.
contract.failure_test: Reject the argument if the count changes under a legal harmless move, if signs are assigned without a shared rule, or if the count is taken before the object and allowed changes are named. A count earns trust only by surviving the allowed changes.

playbook.setup: Start by listing the local events that may change under motion: cells split, crossings appear, turns shift, signs reverse, or defects move. The list tells the count what it must survive and prevents the reader from counting whatever is easiest to see in the first drawing.
playbook.move: Choose a count whose allowed changes cancel by design, using alternating terms, parity, or signs that come from the geometry of the situation. Then test the count on each basic local change before using it globally: what happens when a cell is subdivided, a pair of crossings is born, or a defect moves?
playbook.payoff: Once the protected total is known in one honest version, every legally related version must obey it. Impossibility or forced existence can follow without checking every drawing because the local survival test already covers the redrawings the problem allows.
playbook.failure: The method fails when the count changes under a harmless legal redraw, when signs are assigned without a checkable direction rule, or when the count is treated as evidence before its survival has been tested. Then the arithmetic follows the picture too closely and cannot carry a whole-family conclusion.
playbook.reader_test: Can the reader explain one local change, show why the chosen count stays fixed through that change, name the rule behind any sign or cancellation, and state what conclusion the count can force for the whole problem?

title: Surface bookkeeping
purpose: Connect small patches, boundaries, and holes to whole-surface conclusions.
first_principles: This family treats a surface as a connected ledger. Local behavior can be drawn patch by patch, but the patches must agree when glued back together.

depth.human_problem: The human problem is that surfaces look simple nearby but can behave differently as wholes. This family asks how patches, boundaries, holes, and orientation combine into whole-surface facts that local inspection alone misses completely.
depth.first_principles: Cut the surface into manageable pieces, understand what happens on each piece, and then glue the bookkeeping back together. The global result is not guessed from one patch; it is forced by how all patches fit.
depth.how_it_works: Surface bookkeeping uses decompositions, orientation choices, boundary terms, and cancellation. It is careful about what is local and what is global, because many surface obstructions appear only after a full trip around the object or a full sum over its pieces.
depth.course_examples: The Mobius strip reveals global one-sidedness. Surface classification tracks handles and crosscaps. Euler characteristic records whole-surface type. Poincare-Hopf shows that vector fields must obey the surface's total count. The same surface facts keep reappearing in different language.
depth.failure_mode: The common failure is to reason locally and assume the whole surface behaves the same way. A Mobius strip defeats that assumption immediately, and later orientation-dependent counts fail without global consistency across the surface.

essay: Surface bookkeeping is needed because a surface can lie to local inspection. Every tiny patch of a sphere, torus, disk, or Mobius strip may look like an ordinary piece of paper. The difference appears when patches are glued into a whole: a route may return reversed, a boundary may add a term, a handle may create a new loop, or a missing disk may change what can be filled.

This family teaches the reader to track the whole surface without losing the local pieces. Divide the surface into manageable parts, count or orient those parts, then check what survives when they are put back together. Euler characteristic, boundary orientation, surface classification, and Poincare-Hopf all depend on this discipline.

From first principles, a surface is both local room and global instruction. Local room lets the course draw curves, arrows, neighborhoods, and small crossings. Global instruction says how those local rooms attach to each other. A sphere, torus, and Mobius band can all look locally ordinary while placing different demands on loops, side choices, and vector fields.

The family connects early strip examples to late dynamics. The Mobius strip shows a local side choice failing after a full trip. Euler characteristic shows a surface count surviving many decompositions. Poincare-Hopf shows the same surface count controlling the total defect of an arrow field. The object has changed, but the bookkeeping habit is the same: local facts must be reconciled with the whole surface.

The mathematical principle is that local freedom is not the same as global freedom. A patch may allow an arrow, a side choice, or a sign, while the completed surface refuses to let all those local choices agree at once. Surface bookkeeping is how the course finds the refusal.

contract.input: A surface whose small patches look manageable but whose completed shape may carry holes, boundary behavior, handles, crosscaps, or side reversal. The input must include the whole carrier surface and the rules for how its patches, edges, or cuts fit together.
contract.action: Cut the surface into pieces, track boundary and orientation data on those pieces, and glue the account back into a whole-surface statement. The pieces are useful only when the recombination is honest: shared edges must be matched correctly, boundary terms must not vanish by wish, and side choices must be checked after a full trip.
contract.evidence: The protected evidence is the global surface account: Euler characteristic, orientability, boundary behavior, or a total controlled by the surface. This evidence belongs to the whole surface, not one patch, because the whole surface decides whether the local accounts can agree.
contract.output: The output is a whole-surface conclusion that local inspection alone could not justify. It says what every local choice must obey when the surface is completed, such as whether a side choice returns reversed or whether a total count must match the surface.
contract.failure_test: Reject the argument if it assumes every local choice glues globally, ignores boundary terms, counts before applying gluing rules, or changes the surface while keeping the old name. Those errors replace the real surface with an easier one.

playbook.setup: Start by naming the whole surface and its edge behavior: boundary, handles, crosscaps, holes, orientation, and any gluing instructions. The carrier surface is part of the data, not background scenery, because the same small patch can belong to very different completed surfaces.
playbook.move: Break the surface into manageable pieces, track local information on the pieces, then glue the account back together without losing global restrictions. The recombination is where the surface speaks, because that is where local choices must agree, reverse, cancel, or fail to extend.
playbook.payoff: The conclusion belongs to the whole surface, not to one patch, one drawing, or one chosen decomposition. It explains what local choices must do when completed, such as which totals, side behaviors, route options, or boundary contributions cannot be avoided.
playbook.failure: The method fails when local ordinariness is mistaken for global simplicity, when boundary and orientation data are dropped, or when a cell count is made before the identifications are understood. Small-patch evidence cannot replace the whole surface or the rules that glue it together.
playbook.reader_test: Can the reader point to the full trip, full gluing, or full sum where the global surface constraint appears, state exactly what the local view missed, and name the whole-surface fact that controls the conclusion?

title: Drawing and embedding arguments
purpose: Ask whether connections can live on a chosen surface without forbidden crossings.
first_principles: This family studies room. A page, sphere, torus, or other surface gives routes and limitations. The answer may be decided before a perfect drawing is found.

depth.human_problem: The human problem is to know whether one object can sit inside another without forbidden collisions. A drawing may suggest an answer, but this family asks for a reason that covers every drawing and every legal attempt.
depth.first_principles: Separate the object's required connections from the room supplied by the surrounding surface or space. If every legal placement would force a forbidden meeting, the obstruction belongs to the topology, not to a bad drawing.
depth.how_it_works: Embedding arguments track crossings, over-under information, winding, linking, and surface room. They ask whether deformation can remove intersections or whether a count proves that some relation survives every allowed placement in the space under study.
depth.course_examples: Path puzzles in a disk, planar graph questions, knots and links, and intersection theory all belong here. The family teaches the reader to distinguish accidental crossings from forced ones by checking what legal motion can remove.
depth.failure_mode: The common failure is to confuse a failed attempt with a proof of impossibility. A topological obstruction must show that every legal attempt fails, not only the first drawing tried or the first plausible arrangement.

essay: Drawing and embedding arguments ask whether there is enough room for required connections. A failed drawing is not enough, because a better drawing may exist. The family therefore separates the object that must be placed from the space that must receive it. Which endpoints are fixed? Which crossings are forbidden? Can one strand pass through another? Does the surrounding surface have holes or handles that provide alternate routes?

This is where knots, links, planar graphs, path puzzles, and intersection arguments meet. Each problem asks whether a relation can be removed by legal motion or whether it belongs to the shape of the situation. A crossing on the page may be accidental. A linking relation or forced intersection may survive every attempt to redraw.

From first principles, embedding is a room test. The object has demands: these points must connect, this loop must close, these strands may not pass through each other. The surrounding space has allowances: routes around holes, extra dimensions, boundaries, or a flat page with no overpass. The proof asks whether the allowances can satisfy the demands without violating the rules.

This family also teaches the difference between a drawing and an obstruction. A drawing is one attempt. An obstruction is a reason every legal attempt fails. That reason may be boundary order in a disk, linking in space, a signed intersection count, or a shortage of dimensions. The course keeps returning to this distinction because visual failure alone is too weak.

The important mathematical idea is not drawing skill. It is proving that all legal drawings face the same constraint. The surface or surrounding space supplies only certain routes, and sometimes those routes are not enough. When that happens, the failure belongs to the topology of the placement problem.

contract.input: An object with required connections or loop relations that must live inside a chosen surface or surrounding space. The input includes both the thing placed and the room that receives it: endpoints, strands, loops, forbidden crossings, over-under information, boundary limits, and the surface or space available for routing.
contract.action: Separate accidental crossings from forced ones by using allowed motion, surface room, over-under data, and route information. The action tests the placement problem itself, not drawing skill. It asks whether every legal placement must keep a relation or whether a better legal drawing can remove it.
contract.evidence: The protected evidence is a relation that every legal placement must respect: linking, winding, unavoidable crossing, endpoint order, or unavailable route room. It survives because legal motion cannot erase it without breaking the placement rules.
contract.output: The output is either a legal placement or a proof that no legal placement can avoid the obstruction. The conclusion is about the placement problem itself, so it must cover all legal attempts rather than one failed sketch.
contract.failure_test: Reject the argument if it treats one failed drawing as impossibility, forgets over-under or linking data, changes the receiving surface, or lets strands pass through each other without permission. A flat sketch can lose the relation being proved.

playbook.setup: Start by separating the required object from the surrounding room: which points connect, which loops link, which crossings are forbidden, and what surface or space carries the placement. The room is part of the problem because a plane, sphere, torus, or three-dimensional space permits different routes.
playbook.move: Try legal placements while tracking route relations, over-under information, crossings, winding, endpoint order, and forbidden passages that cannot be erased by allowed motion. The move tests the placement relation, not drawing skill or the neatness of one sketch.
playbook.payoff: The result is either a legal placement or a proof that every legal placement must encounter the same obstruction. A real obstruction defeats all legal attempts, not only the first drawing that comes to mind, because it is tied to the relation the placement must preserve.
playbook.failure: The method fails when one bad drawing is treated as proof, when spatial information such as over-under order is lost in a flat picture, or when the surrounding surface is quietly changed. The missing data may be the whole point, especially for knots, links, and route problems.
playbook.reader_test: Can the reader say why every legal attempt is blocked, rather than only why one attempted drawing failed, name the surrounding room, and identify the placement relation that survives redrawings?

title: Motion through possible states
purpose: Turn mechanical or physical questions into questions about paths and barriers.
first_principles: This family replaces the object in motion with the space of all its possible positions. Holes and walls in that space explain blocked motions, unavoidable coincidences, and forced positions.

depth.human_problem: The human problem is to understand motion when exact equations or trajectories are unavailable. This family asks what the shape of possible states can force before anything is solved second by second or computed point by point.
depth.first_principles: Represent each complete possible state as a point in a new space. Complete means enough information to recover the situation the question cares about: positions, angles, boundary conditions, contacts, and forbidden collisions. Motion becomes a path or rule on that space. Fixed points, equilibria, blocked routes, and forced passages become questions about the shape of the allowed state space.
depth.how_it_works: The family translates physical or dynamical behavior into shape: graph of a rule against self-agreement, vector-field defects, index sums, or paths in a configuration space. Once translated, earlier tools such as deformation and surviving counts apply, but the translation remains part of the proof.
depth.course_examples: The center-of-gravity demonstration, Brouwer fixed point theorem, vector fields, equilibria, Poincare-Hopf, and late applications all use this family. The course ends here because it shows topology acting on behavior, not only on static pictures.
depth.failure_mode: The common failure is to model the state space carelessly. If the states, boundaries, forbidden positions, or allowed motions are wrong, the topological conclusion may no longer describe the physical system being studied at all.

essay: Motion-through-state arguments are the course's bridge from shapes to behavior. Instead of following a mechanism directly, the method lists its possible states and treats each state as a point in a new space. A motion is then a path through that space. A rule becomes a map of the space to itself. A forbidden physical arrangement becomes a wall, hole, or missing region in the state space.

This family explains why fixed points, vector fields, configuration spaces, and physical examples belong with surface topology. They are all ways of asking what behavior the shape of possibility permits. The course does not need every equation of motion to say something meaningful. If the state space has the right obstruction, some positions, coincidences, defects, or blocked motions are forced before detailed solving begins.

From first principles, the method replaces time with possibility. Instead of asking where the system goes at every instant, ask what one complete state is, what states are allowed, and what paths through the state space would represent legal motion. A fixed point becomes self-agreement of a rule on that space. An equilibrium becomes a zero of an arrow field. A blocked motion becomes a missing path. A forbidden collision becomes a removed point, wall, or region that can split the space of possible motions.

The family matters because the same topological tools now speak about behavior. Deformation tracks legal motion through possible states. Invariants record what cannot change along such motion. Fixed-point theorems and index sums force special states. The late applications are not separate from the earlier paper-strip lessons; they use the same object, move, protected fact, and consequence pattern.

The detail that keeps the method honest is modeling. The state space must contain the right freedoms and remove the right forbidden states. One point must not hide two physically different situations unless the problem truly treats them as the same. A path must mean a legal continuous motion, not merely a line drawn in a convenient diagram. If that translation is wrong, the topological conclusion may be true about the model but false about the physical situation. Modeling is therefore part of the proof, not a story attached before the proof begins.

contract.input: A physical or dynamical situation whose direct motion is too complicated to follow point by point. The input must be translated into complete states, not a loose physical impression or a picture that forgets a real degree of freedom. One point of the state space must mean one complete possible situation.
contract.action: Build the space of possible states, remove forbidden states, translate motion into paths or rules, and apply fixed-point, index, or obstruction reasoning there. The action moves from behavior to the shape of possibility while preserving the original freedoms, contacts, boundaries, and forbidden positions.
contract.evidence: The protected evidence is the shape of possibility: a barrier, hole, forced self-agreement, index total, or missing legal path. That evidence constrains behavior without solving every trajectory because each point still means a real possible state and each path still means a legal gradual motion.
contract.output: The output is a constraint on the original motion, such as an unavoidable state, blocked motion, equilibrium, required defect, or forced self-agreement. The conclusion must translate back to the physical setup in the same terms used to build the state space.
contract.failure_test: Reject the argument if the state space leaves out a real freedom, adds a false barrier, keeps forbidden states inside, merges different physical states without permission, or cannot translate the conclusion back to the physical setup.

playbook.setup: Start by listing what information describes one complete state: positions, angles, boundary conditions, contact rules, forbidden collisions, and any rule acting on states. One point should mean one possible situation, not a partial sketch of it or a physical drawing that forgets a real freedom.
playbook.move: Turn those states into a space, remove forbidden states, read motion as paths or maps, and then apply deformation, fixed-point, index, or obstruction reasoning inside that state space. The proof happens in the model, so the model must keep the original freedoms and restrictions all the way through.
playbook.payoff: The original system inherits the conclusion because the state space records the real freedoms and restrictions of the physical or dynamical problem. The result is behavioral, not only geometric: a blocked path, forced state, equilibrium, unavoidable defect, or self-agreement of a rule.
playbook.failure: The method fails when the state space omits a real freedom, adds a false wall, keeps forbidden states inside, merges different physical states without permission, or cannot translate its conclusion back to the original motion.
playbook.reader_test: Can the reader name the state space, say what one point records, list the forbidden states, identify the rule or path, name the topological feature forcing behavior, and translate the conclusion back to the physical setup?
